```{r setup}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(metafor)   # also attaches {metadat}, which holds dat.bcg

source("R/hta_methods.R")

fmt_ci <- function(est, lo, hi, d = 2) {
  f <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)
  paste0(f(est), " (", f(lo), ", ", f(hi), ")")
}
fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))

bcg <- metadat::dat.bcg
k   <- nrow(bcg)
```

## The data

The dataset holds `r k` trials of the BCG vaccine against tuberculosis,
published between 1948 and 1980.
Each row is a 2x2 table: tuberculosis cases and non-cases among vaccinated
and unvaccinated people.

Source: Colditz GA, Brewer TF, Berkey CS, et al. Efficacy of BCG vaccine in
the prevention of tuberculosis. Meta-analysis of the published literature.
*JAMA* 1994, 271(9), 698-702. The data ship with the R package `{metadat}`.

```{r data}
bcg %>%
  transmute(Trial = trial, Author = author, Year = year,
            `Vaccinated: TB / N` = paste0(tpos, " / ", tpos + tneg),
            `Control: TB / N` = paste0(cpos, " / ", cpos + cneg),
            `Absolute latitude` = ablat, Allocation = alloc)
```

## 1. Each trial's effect and standard error

The effect measure is the risk ratio (RR). Meta-analysis works on the log
scale, where the estimate is close to normal and its variance has a simple
form. For a trial with *a* cases among *n1* vaccinated and *c* cases among
*n0* controls:

- log RR = log(*a*/*n1*) - log(*c*/*n0*)
- Var(log RR) = 1/*a* - 1/*n1* + 1/*c* - 1/*n0*

The code computes both by hand, then with `metafor::escalc()`.

```{r escalc}
hand <- bcg %>%
  mutate(n1 = tpos + tneg, n0 = cpos + cneg,
         yi = log(tpos / n1) - log(cpos / n0),
         vi = 1 / tpos - 1 / n1 + 1 / cpos - 1 / n0)

es <- escalc(measure = "RR", ai = tpos, bi = tneg, ci = cpos, di = cneg, data = bcg)

data.frame(Trial = bcg$trial,
           `log RR, hand` = round(hand$yi, 4), `SE, hand` = round(sqrt(hand$vi), 4),
           `RR (95% CI)` = fmt_ci(exp(hand$yi), exp(hand$yi - 1.96 * sqrt(hand$vi)),
                                  exp(hand$yi + 1.96 * sqrt(hand$vi))),
           check.names = FALSE)
```

Largest difference between hand and `escalc()`: log RR
`r sprintf("%.1e", max(abs(hand$yi - es$yi)))`, variance
`r sprintf("%.1e", max(abs(hand$vi - es$vi)))`. The test suite checks the same
values with tolerance 1e-8.

## 2. Fixed-effect pooled estimate

The fixed-effect model assumes that all trials estimate one common true
effect. Differences between trials are then sampling error only. The best
estimate is a weighted mean with weights *w~i~* = 1/*v~i~*, the inverse of each
trial's variance. Large trials get large weights.

- pooled log RR = Σ *w~i~ y~i~* / Σ *w~i~*
- SE = 1 / √(Σ *w~i~*)

```{r fe}
fe  <- fe_hand(es$yi, es$vi)
fe_pkg <- rma(yi, vi, data = es, method = "FE")

# Share of the total weight per trial, for the text.
weights_tab <- bcg %>%
  mutate(n = tpos + tneg + cpos + cneg,
         w_fe = 100 * (1 / es$vi) / sum(1 / es$vi))
w_top <- weights_tab %>% slice_max(w_fe, n = 1)

data.frame(
  Source = c("Hand", "metafor::rma(method = \"FE\")"),
  `Pooled log RR` = c(fe$est, fe_pkg$beta[1]),
  SE = c(fe$se, fe_pkg$se),
  `Pooled RR (95% CI)` = c(fmt_ci(exp(fe$est), exp(fe$lower), exp(fe$upper)),
                           fmt_ci(exp(fe_pkg$beta[1]), exp(fe_pkg$ci.lb), exp(fe_pkg$ci.ub))),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

The fixed-effect estimate is RR `r fmt_ci(exp(fe$est), exp(fe$lower), exp(fe$upper))`.
The weights are very unequal. The largest trial, `r w_top$author` `r w_top$year`
with `r format(w_top$n, big.mark = ",")` participants, carries
`r sprintf("%.0f", w_top$w_fe)`% of the weight on its own.

## 3. Random-effects model

```{r re}
# Tight convergence so that the package and the hand REML agree to 1e-8.
re_pkg <- rma(yi, vi, data = es, method = "REML", test = "knha",
              control = list(threshold = 1e-12, maxiter = 1000))
tau2   <- reml_tau2_hand(es$yi, es$vi)
re     <- re_hand(es$yi, es$vi, tau2, knha = TRUE)
pred   <- predict(re_pkg)

data.frame(
  Quantity = c("tau^2 (REML)", "Pooled log RR", "SE (Hartung-Knapp)",
               "95% CI, lower", "95% CI, upper", "Prediction interval, lower",
               "Prediction interval, upper"),
  Hand = c(tau2, re$est, re$se, re$lower, re$upper, re$pi_lower, re$pi_upper),
  metafor = c(re_pkg$tau2, re_pkg$beta[1], re_pkg$se, re_pkg$ci.lb, re_pkg$ci.ub,
              pred$pi.lb, pred$pi.ub)
)
```

The random-effects model assumes that each trial has its own true effect.
These true effects vary around a mean, with between-trial variance τ².
REML (restricted maximum likelihood) estimates τ². The hand version uses
Fisher scoring, as `metafor` does. The Hartung-Knapp adjustment then rescales
the standard error by the observed spread of the trials around the mean. It
uses a *t* distribution with *k* - 1 = `r k - 1` degrees of freedom. That gives
more honest coverage when there are few trials.

IQWiG uses the same Knapp-Hartung method but estimates τ² by the
Paule-Mandel method (General Methods 7.0, section 9.3.7). Section 7 below
runs the analysis that way on an oncology example.

**Fixed effect against random effects, in five sentences.**
The fixed-effect model asks what the one common effect is, and it treats all
differences between trials as chance.
The random-effects model asks what the average effect is across a population
of settings whose true effects differ.
It adds τ² to every trial's variance, so the weights become more equal and
small trials gain influence.
Its confidence interval is wider because it carries the uncertainty about
the spread of effects as well as the sampling error.
When τ² is zero the two models give the same answer.

Here the random-effects estimate is RR
`r fmt_ci(exp(re$est), exp(re$lower), exp(re$upper))`. The fixed-effect
estimate was `r fmt_ci(exp(fe$est), exp(fe$lower), exp(fe$upper))`. The two
differ because of the weights. The largest trial found no benefit (RR
`r sprintf("%.2f", exp(es$yi[w_top$trial]))`) and carries
`r sprintf("%.0f", w_top$w_fe)`% of the fixed-effect weight. The random-effects
weights are more equal, and most smaller trials found larger benefits.

## 4. Heterogeneity

```{r het}
het <- heterogeneity_hand(es$yi, es$vi, tau2)

data.frame(
  Statistic = c("Q (df)", "p-value for Q", "tau^2", "tau", "I^2", "H^2",
                "Prediction interval for the RR"),
  Value = c(sprintf("%.1f (%d)", het$Q, het$df), fmt_p(het$Qp), sprintf("%.3f", het$tau2),
            sprintf("%.3f", sqrt(het$tau2)), sprintf("%.1f%%", het$I2), sprintf("%.1f", het$H2),
            sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", exp(re$pi_lower), exp(re$pi_upper))),
  `Question it answers` = c(
    "Do the trials differ by more than chance would allow?",
    "How surprising is that spread if there were one common effect?",
    "How large is the spread of true effects, on the log RR scale?",
    "The same, as a standard deviation (easier to read).",
    "What share of the total variation is real difference between trials?",
    "How many times larger the total variation is than sampling error alone.",
    "Where would the true effect of a new, similar trial lie?"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

- **Q** is a test. With few trials it has little power, and with many
  trials it flags trivial differences. A large p-value does not show that the
  trials agree.
- **I²** is a share, not an amount. With large, precise trials even a small
  τ² gives a high I². With small trials a large τ² can give a low I². `metafor` computes it from τ². The
  classic formula (Q - df)/Q = `r sprintf("%.1f%%", het$I2_from_Q)` gives the
  same value only with the DerSimonian-Laird τ².
- **τ²** is the amount. It is on the scale of the effect, so it can be
  judged clinically: τ = `r sprintf("%.2f", sqrt(tau2))` on the log scale means true risk
  ratios that differ by a factor of about
  `r sprintf("%.1f", exp(2 * 1.96 * sqrt(tau2)))` between the 2.5th and 97.5th
  percentile.
- **The prediction interval** turns τ² into a statement about practice. Here
  it runs from `r sprintf("%.2f", exp(re$pi_lower))` to
  `r sprintf("%.2f", exp(re$pi_upper))`. It includes 1, so in some new setting
  the vaccine might not protect at all, even though the mean effect is clearly
  protective. With the Hartung-Knapp adjustment, `metafor` uses a *t*
  distribution with *k* - 1 degrees of freedom here. Some texts use *k* - 2.

Latitude is a known candidate effect modifier in these trials. Colditz and
colleagues found larger benefits further from the equator. A meta-regression
on absolute latitude shows how much of τ² it explains.

```{r metareg}
mr <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ ablat, data = es, method = "REML", test = "knha")
data.frame(
  Model = c("No covariate", "Absolute latitude"),
  `tau^2` = round(c(re_pkg$tau2, mr$tau2), 3),
  `Change in log RR per 10 degrees` = c("", sprintf("%.3f (95%% CI %.3f, %.3f)",
                                       10 * mr$beta[2], 10 * mr$ci.lb[2], 10 * mr$ci.ub[2])),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

Latitude explains about `r round(100 * (1 - mr$tau2 / re_pkg$tau2))`% of the
between-trial variance. This is the same idea as an effect modifier in
chapter 3. A variable that changes the effect, and is distributed
differently across trials, produces heterogeneity.

## 5. Forest plot, funnel plot and leave-one-out

```{r forest, fig.height = 6.5}
forest(re_pkg, atransf = exp, addpred = TRUE, header = c("Trial", "RR [95% CI]"),
       slab = paste(bcg$author, bcg$year), refline = 0,
       xlab = "Risk ratio (log scale), below 1 favours vaccination",
       mlab = "Random effects, REML, Hartung-Knapp")
```

The diamond is the pooled estimate and its confidence interval. The dotted
line under it is the prediction interval. Square size shows each trial's
weight in the random-effects model.

```{r funnel, fig.height = 4.5}
funnel(re_pkg, atransf = exp, xlab = "Risk ratio (log scale)")
egger <- regtest(re_pkg)
```

The funnel plot shows each trial's effect against its standard error. Small
trials scatter more widely. Without small-study effects such as publication
bias, the points form a symmetric funnel. Egger's regression test gives
p = `r sprintf("%.2f", egger$pval)`. With `r k` trials the test has little
power, and asymmetry can also come from real heterogeneity. So the funnel
plot is a check, not a proof either way.

```{r loo}
loo <- leave1out(re_pkg, transf = exp)
data.frame(`Trial left out` = paste(bcg$author, bcg$year),
           `Pooled RR (95% CI)` = fmt_ci(loo$estimate, loo$ci.lb, loo$ci.ub),
           `tau^2` = round(loo$tau2, 3),
           `I^2, %` = round(loo$I2, 1),
           check.names = FALSE)
```

Leaving out one trial at a time moves the pooled RR only between
`r sprintf("%.2f", min(loo$estimate))` and `r sprintf("%.2f", max(loo$estimate))`.
No single trial drives the conclusion that the vaccine protects on average.

## 6. A random-effects meta-analysis is a mixed model

The random-effects model is a linear mixed model with one observation per
trial:

*y~i~* = μ + *u~i~* + *e~i~*, with *u~i~* ~ N(0, τ²) and *e~i~* ~ N(0, *v~i~*).

μ is the fixed intercept, the pooled effect. *u~i~* is a random intercept per
trial, with variance τ². *e~i~* is the residual, but unlike an ordinary mixed
model its variance *v~i~* is known from each trial and not estimated. That is
why `lme4::lmer()` cannot fit it directly. `lmer()` always estimates a
residual variance, and its weights only rescale it.
`metafor::rma.mv()` is a general mixed-model fitter that accepts known
residual variances. Fitting the trial as a random intercept reproduces the
REML random-effects model.

```{r mixed}
mv <- rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ 1 | trial, data = es, method = "REML",
             control = list(optimizer = "optim", optmethod = "BFGS",
                            optCtrl = list(reltol = 1e-14)))
re_z <- rma(yi, vi, data = es, method = "REML",
            control = list(threshold = 1e-12, maxiter = 1000))

data.frame(
  Model = c("rma(), random effects", "rma.mv(), random intercept per trial"),
  `tau^2 / sigma^2` = c(re_z$tau2, mv$sigma2),
  `mu (pooled log RR)` = c(re_z$beta[1], mv$beta[1]),
  SE = c(re_z$se, mv$se),
  `REML log-likelihood` = c(logLik(re_z), logLik(mv)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

The two fits agree to about seven decimal places. The small remaining
difference comes from two different numerical optimisers, not from the
model. The test suite therefore checks this pair with tolerance 1e-6. The
hand calculations are checked with tolerance 1e-8.

What carries over from mixed models: τ² is the random-intercept variance,
REML is used for the same reason as in any mixed model, and the prediction
interval is the spread of a new random intercept. What differs: there is one
row per trial and no individual patient data, so the within-trial variance
has to be supplied. With individual patient data, the same question becomes
a one-stage model, for example `lme4::glmer()` with a random treatment
effect per trial.

## 7. Pooling hazard ratios: chemotherapy in head and neck cancer

An oncology HTA team pools hazard ratios, not risk ratios. The method is the
same once each trial's log hazard ratio and its variance are known. Only the
first step differs.

The data come from the MACH-NC meta-analysis of individual patient data:
`r nrow(metadat::dat.pignon2000)` randomised trials of locoregional treatment
with chemotherapy against locoregional treatment alone in head and neck
squamous-cell carcinoma. The outcome is death. Source: Pignon JP, Bourhis J,
Domenge C, Designe L. Chemotherapy added to locoregional treatment for head
and neck squamous-cell carcinoma: three meta-analyses of updated individual
data. *Lancet* 2000, 355(9208), 949-955.

### Each trial's log hazard ratio

With individual patient data, each trial gives the log-rank statistics for
the chemotherapy arm: the observed minus expected number of deaths (O - E)
and its variance V. Then log HR = (O - E) / V and Var(log HR) = 1 / V. This
is the Peto method, standard in individual patient data meta-analyses of
survival.

From published papers one usually has only the hazard ratio and its 95%
confidence interval. The standard error then follows from the width of the
interval on the log scale: SE = (log upper - log lower) / (2 × 1.96). The
code shows that the two routes give the same answer, by building each
trial's interval and recovering the standard error from it.

```{r pignon-effects}
pig <- metadat::dat.pignon2000
hr  <- loghr_from_ome(pig$OmE, pig$V)
pig$yi <- hr$yi
pig$vi <- hr$vi
pig$timing <- factor(pig$grp, levels = 1:3,
                     labels = c("Adjuvant", "Neoadjuvant", "Concomitant"))

# Published-style summary: HR and 95% CI, then back to the standard error.
pub <- data.frame(hr = exp(pig$yi),
                  lower = exp(pig$yi - qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(pig$vi)),
                  upper = exp(pig$yi + qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(pig$vi)))
back <- loghr_from_ci(pub$hr, pub$lower, pub$upper)

head(data.frame(Trial = pig$trial, Timing = pig$timing, `O - E` = pig$OmE, V = pig$V,
                `HR (95% CI)` = fmt_ci(pub$hr, pub$lower, pub$upper),
                `SE from O - E and V` = round(sqrt(pig$vi), 4),
                `SE from the CI` = round(back$se, 4), check.names = FALSE), 8)
```

Largest difference between the two standard errors over all trials:
`r sprintf("%.1e", max(abs(back$se - sqrt(pig$vi))))`.

### Pooling the way IQWiG does

IQWiG's General Methods (version 7.0, section 9.3.7) describe the steps.

1. If heterogeneity cannot be excluded, use a random-effects model.
2. With enough studies, use the Knapp-Hartung method and estimate τ² by
   Paule-Mandel.
3. Run DerSimonian-Laird as a sensitivity analysis. If the Knapp-Hartung
   interval is narrower than the DerSimonian-Laird one, apply the ad hoc
   variance correction of Knapp and Hartung.
4. With fewer than 5 studies, τ² cannot be estimated reliably. A
   fixed-effect model or a qualitative summary is then considered.

The Paule-Mandel τ² is the value at which the generalised Q statistic equals
its expected value, *k* - 1. The code finds it by hand with a root search
and compares it with `metafor`.

```{r pignon-pool}
fe_pig  <- fe_hand(pig$yi, pig$vi)
tau2_pm <- pm_tau2_hand(pig$yi, pig$vi)
kh      <- rma(yi, vi, data = pig, method = "PM", test = "knha",
               control = list(tol = 1e-14))
dl      <- rma(yi, vi, data = pig, method = "DL")
use_adhoc <- (kh$ci.ub - kh$ci.lb) < (dl$ci.ub - dl$ci.lb)
final   <- if (use_adhoc) rma(yi, vi, data = pig, method = "PM", test = "adhoc") else kh
re_pig  <- re_hand(pig$yi, pig$vi, tau2_pm, knha = TRUE)
het_pig <- heterogeneity_hand(pig$yi, pig$vi, tau2_pm)

data.frame(
  Model = c("Fixed effect (inverse variance)", "DerSimonian-Laird",
            "Paule-Mandel with Knapp-Hartung (IQWiG)"),
  `tau^2` = c("", sprintf("%.4f", dl$tau2),
              sprintf("%.4f (hand %.4f)", kh$tau2, tau2_pm)),
  `Pooled HR (95% CI)` = c(fmt_ci(exp(fe_pig$est), exp(fe_pig$lower), exp(fe_pig$upper)),
                           fmt_ci(exp(dl$beta[1]), exp(dl$ci.lb), exp(dl$ci.ub)),
                           fmt_ci(exp(re_pig$est), exp(re_pig$lower), exp(re_pig$upper))),
  `CI width (log scale)` = sprintf("%.3f", c(fe_pig$upper - fe_pig$lower,
                                             dl$ci.ub - dl$ci.lb, kh$ci.ub - kh$ci.lb)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

The Knapp-Hartung interval is `r ifelse(use_adhoc, "narrower", "wider")`
than the DerSimonian-Laird interval, so the ad hoc variance correction
`r ifelse(use_adhoc, "is", "is not")` needed. Chemotherapy reduces the hazard
of death to about `r sprintf("%.2f", exp(re_pig$est))` times that without
chemotherapy, 95% CI `r sprintf("%.2f", exp(re_pig$lower))` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", exp(re_pig$upper))`. Heterogeneity is moderate: I² =
`r sprintf("%.0f", het_pig$I2)`%, and the prediction interval for a new trial
runs from `r sprintf("%.2f", exp(re_pig$pi_lower))` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", exp(re_pig$pi_upper))`.

### Does the timing of chemotherapy matter?

The trials gave chemotherapy at three times: after locoregional treatment
(adjuvant), before it (neoadjuvant) or together with radiotherapy
(concomitant). This is a subgroup analysis across trials. The test for
subgroup differences compares the spread between the subgroup estimates
with what chance would allow. Under the fixed-effect model it is the total
Q minus the Q within each subgroup.

```{r pignon-subgroups}
qb   <- q_between_hand(pig$yi, pig$vi, pig$timing)
qb_p <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ timing, data = pig, method = "FE")
mr_p <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ timing, data = pig, method = "PM", test = "knha")

by_timing <- bind_rows(lapply(levels(pig$timing), function(t) {
  d <- pig[pig$timing == t, ]
  f <- fe_hand(d$yi, d$vi)
  data.frame(Timing = t, Trials = nrow(d),
             `Pooled HR, fixed effect (95% CI)` = fmt_ci(exp(f$est), exp(f$lower), exp(f$upper)),
             est = f$est, lo = f$lower, hi = f$upper, check.names = FALSE)
}))
by_timing %>% select(-est, -lo, -hi)
```

Test for subgroup differences, fixed effect: Q = `r sprintf("%.2f", qb$Q_between)`
on `r qb$df` degrees of freedom, p = `r fmt_p(qb$p)` (hand), and
`r sprintf("%.2f", qb_p$QM)` from `metafor`. With random effects and
Knapp-Hartung, the test from a meta-regression on timing gives
p = `r fmt_p(mr_p$QMp)`.

```{r pignon-forest, fig.height = 3}
fd <- bind_rows(by_timing %>% select(label = Timing, est, lo, hi),
                data.frame(label = "All trials (Paule-Mandel, Knapp-Hartung)",
                           est = re_pig$est, lo = re_pig$lower, hi = re_pig$upper)) %>%
  mutate(label = factor(label, levels = rev(label)))
ggplot(fd, aes(exp(est), label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = exp(lo), xmax = exp(hi)), width = 0.2, orientation = "y") +
  geom_point(shape = 18, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Hazard ratio of death, chemotherapy vs none (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

Only concomitant chemotherapy shows a clear benefit. That was the main
finding of the original publication. Two cautions apply, and an assessor
would raise both. Timing was not randomised within trials, so the
comparison between subgroups is observational and can be confounded by
other differences between the trials. And the subgroup was one of several
possible splits, so a single significant test needs to have been planned in
advance to carry weight.
